title: Rantideva's last meal
hookLine: a starving king gives his last meal and water to whoever knocks
carry: give with faith; the guest is god

cards: A king named Rantideva has given away so much that he and his family have nothing left. The Bhagavata Purana says they went forty-eight days without food, and without even water.
On the forty-ninth morning, someone brings them a little: rice cooked in milk, some ghee, some water. They sit down to eat at last. And there's a knock.
A guest is at the door, and he's hungry.

teach.h: A GUEST. A LABORER. A MAN WITH DOGS.
teach.b: Rantideva shares his food with the guest, honoring him. Then a second guest comes, a poor laborer, and he shares again.
Then a man arrives with a pack of hungry dogs, and Rantideva gives him the rest of the food and bows to the man and the dogs alike.

teach.h: THE LAST WATER, TO AN OUTCASTE.
teach.b: Only the water is left. Then an outcaste comes, a man the society of that time wouldn't even touch, and says he's dying of thirst. Rantideva, nearly dying of thirst himself, gives him the water.
The Purana gives him a prayer at that moment: he doesn't ask God for powers, or even for freedom from rebirth; he asks to take on the pain of every creature, so that they can be free of it.
Then the guests show who they really were: the lords of the three worlds, come to test him.
He bows, and he asks them for nothing. That's dana, giving, as Hindu texts hold it up.

teach.h: ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: THE GUEST IS GOD.
teach.b: The Taittiriya Upanishad, in its parting advice to students, says: treat the guest as God, atithi devo bhava. A line later: give with faith. The Gita's seventeenth chapter sorts gifts three ways.
The clear gift is given because giving is right, to someone who can't repay you.
The restless gift wants something back, or comes with a wince. The heavy gift comes with contempt. It's why so many Hindu homes won't let a guest leave hungry.
Today the guest is your kid's friend at dinner, the new coworker, the driver at your door: the same welcome, no bill attached.

how: Many Hindu homes treat a guest as God (atithi devo bhava), feed whoever arrives and set aside food before a meal; dana, giving, is a daily and festival duty, and Gita 17.20–22 and the Taittiriya Upanishad's 'give with faith' are often quoted on how a gift should be given.

o: a gift given to be thanked and remembered
action, like a gift given just because it's right
the amount of money a gift is worth

p: gave his last meal to his guests
received the last of the water

s: when the gods revealed themselves, Rantideva asked them for a reward
he bowed and asked for nothing; his mind stayed on God.
a gift given expecting a return is the restless kind
Gita 17.21: given for a return or reward, or grudgingly.
the Taittiriya Upanishad says to treat the guest as God
atithi devo bhava. and a line later: shraddhaya deyam, give with faith.

games.q: you're Rantideva. after forty-eight days without food, you finally sit down to eat, and a hungry stranger knocks. what did he do?
o: ate first, then shared what was left.
shared his meal, and kept giving to each one who came.
asked the stranger to come back tomorrow.
games.why: he fed a guest, a laborer, a man with dogs, and gave his last water to an outcaste. they were the lords of the three worlds, and he asked them for nothing.

practice: Picture the next meal you'll eat. Many Hindu homes set aside a little food before anyone eats: for a guest, a hungry person, a cow, the birds.
Decide where a first portion of yours could go this week, a meal, an hour, a seat at your table, and who might receive it.
If you pray, offer the meal to God first, as Rantideva saw God in each guest; if you don't, give quiet thanks for whoever it reaches.

wordCard.voice: Karma. Action. Rantideva's action was the simplest gift there is: his own meal, given to whoever knocked, asking nothing back.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a gift, giving; the word behind the Gita's three kinds of gift (17.20–22).

carryVoice: Your line: give with faith; the guest is God. Rantideva gave his last meal and asked for nothing. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 9.21 (Rantideva's forty-eight-day fast; his food and water given to four guests; his prayer; the lords of the three worlds), retold
